task: Choose the correct form: She ___ in a bank.
wrong options / checks: work | is work | working
explanation shown to learner: With he, she and it we add -s to the verb: she works.

task: Which sentence is about a habit (something you do again and again)?
wrong options / checks: I am drinking tea now. | I drank tea yesterday. | I will drink tea tomorrow.
explanation shown to learner: 'Every morning' shows a habit. We use the present simple for habits and routines.

task: My brother ___ football. (not / like)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: does not like
explanation shown to learner: With he, she, it we use doesn't + the base verb: he doesn't like.

task: Make it negative: They play tennis on Sundays.
correct answer: They don't play tennis on Sundays.
wrong options / checks: also accepted: They do not play tennis on Sundays.
explanation shown to learner: With I, you, we, they we make the negative with don't + base verb.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: He plays the guitar. | Do you like pizza? | We live in Riga.
explanation shown to learner: With 'she' we say doesn't: She doesn't work on Sunday.

task: A friend writes: 'Does he works here?' What is the best advice?
correct answer: Write 'Does he work here?' After does we use the base verb.
wrong options / checks: The sentence is correct. Do not change it. | Write 'Do he works here?' | Write 'Is he works here?'
explanation shown to learner: In questions the helper verb (do/does) shows the person. The main verb stays in the base form: Does he work?

task: Write one sentence about what your friend or colleague does every day. Start with He or She.
correct answer: She starts work at eight every day.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use he or she + a verb with -s, for example: she starts work at eight. ; Add a time word such as every day, usually or always.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Choose the correct word: Where ___ your sister work?
wrong options / checks: do | is | works
explanation shown to learner: Questions in the present simple: do/does + subject + base verb. Sister = she, so does.

task: Which sentence is about a timetable?
wrong options / checks: The train is leaving now. | The train left at 7.45 yesterday. | I am on the train.
explanation shown to learner: We use the present simple for fixed timetables, even for the future.

task: What time ___ the film ___? (start)
explanation shown to learner: Question: What time + does + subject + base verb.

task: Make a question with How: She goes to work by bus.
correct answer: How does she go to work?
wrong options / checks: also accepted: How does she get to work?
explanation shown to learner: Question: How + does + she + base verb. The -es goes away: goes becomes go.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: My sister never eats fish. | He doesn't have a car. | We usually go by bus.
explanation shown to learner: After do we need the base verb: Do they speak English?

task: Your colleague says: 'He go to the gym on Mondays.' What is the best advice?
correct answer: Say 'He goes to the gym on Mondays.' Add -es for he, she, it.
wrong options / checks: Say 'He go to the gym on Mondays.' It is correct. | Say 'He is go to the gym on Mondays.' | Say 'He going to the gym on Mondays.'
explanation shown to learner: With he, she, it the present simple verb takes -s or -es: he goes.

task: Write a question to ask a new colleague about their free time. Start with Do you or What do you.
correct answer: What do you usually do at the weekend?
wrong options / checks: must contain: Start with Do you ... or What do you ... ; End the question with a question mark.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Which verb do we NOT usually use with -ing?
wrong options / checks: run | swim | jump
explanation shown to learner: Verbs of thinking, feeling and having (know, like, want, need, believe) are state verbs. We use the present simple: I know.

task: Which sentence is a general truth (always true)?
wrong options / checks: The water is boiling now. | The water boiled yesterday. | I'm boiling water for tea.
explanation shown to learner: We use the present simple for facts and things that are always true.

task: Our flight ___ at 6.40 tomorrow morning. (leave)
explanation shown to learner: The present simple is used for timetables, even for the future: the flight leaves.

task: Make it negative and use 'any': She has money.
wrong options / checks: also accepted: She does not have any money. | She hasn't any money. | She has not any money.
explanation shown to learner: Negative: doesn't + base verb. With 'any' for uncountable or plural nouns.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: The museum opens at nine. | How much does it cost? | He doesn't speak French.
explanation shown to learner: 'Like' is a state verb. We say: I like this song.

task: Your friend says: 'I'm wanting a coffee.' What is the best correction?
correct answer: 'I want a coffee.' Want is a state verb, so we use the present simple.
wrong options / checks: 'I'm wanting a coffee.' It is correct. | 'I wanted a coffee now.' | 'I am want a coffee.'
explanation shown to learner: State verbs (want, need, like, know) are normally not used in the continuous.

task: Write two sentences about your timetable for tomorrow (work or class). Use the present simple with a time.
correct answer: My class starts at 9.00. It finishes at 11.30.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use a timetable verb (starts, finishes, leaves ...) with 'at' and a time. ; Write two sentences.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Look! The children ___ in the garden.
wrong options / checks: play | is playing | plays
explanation shown to learner: Right now: am/is/are + verb-ing. 'The children' = they, so are playing.

task: Which sentence is happening right now?
wrong options / checks: I cook dinner every day. | I cooked dinner yesterday. | I will cook dinner tomorrow.
explanation shown to learner: The present continuous shows an action in progress now.

task: Shh! The baby ___. (sleep)
explanation shown to learner: Now: is + sleeping. The baby = it.

task: She ___ in the park now. (run)
explanation shown to learner: Spelling: run becomes running (we double the n).

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: He is watching TV. | I am reading a book. | We are having lunch.
explanation shown to learner: After are we need verb-ing: They are playing football.

task: A friend is at the station and you ask about now. Which question is best?
wrong options / checks: What do you do now? | What you are doing now? | What are you do now?
explanation shown to learner: For right now we use are + you + verb-ing.

task: Look around you. Write one sentence about what you are doing now. Start with I am.
correct answer: I am sitting at my desk.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use I am (or I'm) + verb-ing, for example: I am sitting at my desk.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: My brother ___ for an exam this week, so he is very busy.
wrong options / checks: studies | study | studying
explanation shown to learner: A temporary situation around now: am/is/are + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence is about a plan for the future?
correct answer: I'm meeting Anna tomorrow at five.
wrong options / checks: I meet Anna every Friday. | I met Anna yesterday. | Anna is my friend.
explanation shown to learner: The present continuous with a future time word shows a fixed plan.

task: What ___ you ___ this weekend? (do)
explanation shown to learner: Question: What + are + you + verb-ing.

task: Make it negative: They are waiting for the bus.
correct answer: They aren't waiting for the bus.
wrong options / checks: also accepted: They are not waiting for the bus.
explanation shown to learner: Negative: am/is/are + not + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: Are you coming to the party? | We aren't working today. | It is raining.
explanation shown to learner: After is we need verb-ing: She is having a shower.

task: Your friend is in Riga for one month only. Which sentence is best?
correct answer: I'm living in a small flat this month.
wrong options / checks: I live in a small flat this month. | I lived in a small flat this month. | I will living in a small flat.
explanation shown to learner: The continuous shows a temporary situation.

task: Write a question to ask a friend about their plans for tonight. Use Are you + verb-ing.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use Are you + verb-ing, for example: Are you going out tonight? ; End the question with a question mark.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Please be quiet. I ___ to concentrate.
wrong options / checks: try | tries | trying
explanation shown to learner: An action in progress at the moment of speaking: am + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence describes a change that is happening now?
wrong options / checks: The weather is cold in winter. | It was cold yesterday. | It gets cold in winter every year.
explanation shown to learner: We use the present continuous for changes in progress: getting colder, growing, rising.

task: These days more people ___ from home. (work)
explanation shown to learner: A trend around now: are + verb-ing.

task: Make a question with Why: He is shouting.
explanation shown to learner: Question word + is + subject + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: She is wanting a new phone.
wrong options / checks: I'm having a great time here. | We're meeting at six. | The prices are going up.
explanation shown to learner: 'Want' is a state verb. We say: She wants a new phone.

task: Is this statement true? 'I'm living with my parents at the moment' sounds more temporary than 'I live with my parents.'
correct answer: Yes. The continuous shows that the situation is temporary.
wrong options / checks: No. They mean exactly the same. | No. Only 'live' can show a temporary situation. | Yes, but only for children.
explanation shown to learner: The present continuous often shows that something is temporary or changing.

task: Write one sentence about a change in your life or your city these days. Use the present continuous.
correct answer: More people are working from home these days.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use am/is/are + verb-ing. ; Add a time phrase such as these days or at the moment.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Yesterday I ___ to the cinema.
wrong options / checks: go | goed | going
explanation shown to learner: Go is irregular. The past form is went.

task: Which sentence is about something finished in the past?
wrong options / checks: We visit Rome every year. | We are visiting Rome. | We will visit Rome.
explanation shown to learner: 'Last year' is a finished time. We use the past simple.

task: She ___ TV last night. (not / watch)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: did not watch
explanation shown to learner: Negative past simple: didn't + base verb.

task: Make a question: He played football.
explanation shown to learner: Question: Did + subject + base verb.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: She visited her aunt. | We watched a film. | He had breakfast at 7.
explanation shown to learner: After didn't use the base verb: I didn't go to school.

task: A friend writes: 'I buyed a new phone yesterday.' What is the best advice?
correct answer: Write 'I bought a new phone.' Buy is irregular: bought.
wrong options / checks: Write 'I buy a new phone yesterday.' | Write 'I did bought a new phone.' | The sentence is correct.
explanation shown to learner: Many common verbs are irregular. You must learn them: buy - bought, go - went, see - saw.

task: Write one sentence about what you did yesterday. Use a past verb and the word yesterday.
correct answer: Yesterday I met a friend for coffee.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use a verb in the past (for example: met, went, worked). ; Use the word yesterday.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Where ___ you ___ last summer?
wrong options / checks: do ... went | did ... went | were ... go
explanation shown to learner: Past simple questions: did + subject + base verb.

task: Which words usually go with the past simple?
correct answer: yesterday, last week, three days ago
wrong options / checks: already, yet, just | now, at the moment, these days | always, usually, never
explanation shown to learner: Finished time words (yesterday, last week, ago) go with the past simple.

task: We ___ late because the bus ___ slow. (be)
explanation shown to learner: Be in the past: I/he/she/it was, you/we/they were.

task: He ___ at 7 and ___ a shower. (wake up / have)
explanation shown to learner: Both verbs are irregular: wake - woke, have - had.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: I met her two years ago. | They didn't like the food. | What did he say?
explanation shown to learner: After did we use the base verb: Did you see the match?

task: A colleague asks: 'What did you do at the weekend?' Which answer is best?
correct answer: I went hiking with my brother.
wrong options / checks: I go hiking with my brother. | I am going hiking with my brother. | I have gone hiking with my brother.
explanation shown to learner: The question is in the past simple, so we answer about a finished time with the past simple.

task: Write two short sentences about your last holiday or day off. Use the past simple.
correct answer: I went to the sea. We swam every day.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use verbs in the past simple (went, stayed, visited ...). ; Write two sentences.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Last year, they ___ married in Paris.
wrong options / checks: get | getting | gotten
explanation shown to learner: Get is irregular. The past simple form is got.

task: Which sentence shows two actions, one after the other, in the past?
correct answer: She opened the door and walked in.
wrong options / checks: She was opening the door and walking in. | She opens the door and walks in. | She has opened the door and has walked in.
explanation shown to learner: We use the past simple for a series of finished actions in order.

task: I ___ Tom at the party, so I called him later. (not / see)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: did not see
explanation shown to learner: Negative: didn't + base verb.

task: Make a question with When: She moved to London.
correct answer: When did she move to London?
explanation shown to learner: Question word + did + subject + base verb.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: Why did you went home early?
wrong options / checks: I didn't have time yesterday. | When did they arrive? | She called me at six.
explanation shown to learner: After did we use the base verb: Why did you go home early?

task: You want to say your report was finished in March. Which sentence is best?
wrong options / checks: I have finished it in March. | I am finishing it in March. | I finish it in March.
explanation shown to learner: 'In March' is a finished time, so we use the past simple, not the present perfect.

task: Write two sentences that start a story. Say what happened first and what happened next (use Then or After that).
correct answer: I got up late. Then I missed the bus.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use Then or After that to show the order. ; Use verbs in the past simple.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Which sentence is correct?
correct answer: We used to play in the park every day.
wrong options / checks: We use to play in the park every day. | We used to playing in the park every day. | We were used to play in the park every day.
explanation shown to learner: Past habits: used to + base verb.

task: What does 'I used to smoke' tell us?
correct answer: I smoked in the past, but I don't smoke now.
wrong options / checks: I smoke now, but not very often. | I am starting to smoke. | I will smoke in the future.
explanation shown to learner: Used to talks about past habits or states that are no longer true.

task: Did you ___ to live in a flat? (use)
explanation shown to learner: In questions and negatives we write 'use to' (not 'used to'): Did you use to ...?

task: He ___ to like fish, but now he loves it. (not / use)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: did not use
explanation shown to learner: Negative: didn't use to + base verb.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I didn't used to like coffee.
wrong options / checks: She used to live in Paris. | Did you use to play chess? | They used to work here.
explanation shown to learner: After didn't we write 'use to': I didn't use to like coffee.

task: Which sentence is best to talk about a repeated habit in the past?
correct answer: As a child, I used to visit my grandparents every summer.
wrong options / checks: As a child, I visited my grandparents last summer. | As a child, I am visiting my grandparents every summer. | As a child, I have visited my grandparents every summer.
explanation shown to learner: 'Used to' + 'every summer' shows a repeated past habit.

task: Write one sentence about something you used to do as a child, but don't do now.
correct answer: I used to collect stickers, but I don't collect them now.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use used to + base verb. ; Add but ... now ... to show it has changed.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: At 8 o'clock yesterday I ___ dinner.
wrong options / checks: cooked | am cooking | were cooking
explanation shown to learner: An action in progress at a moment in the past: was/were + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence shows an action in progress at a moment in the past?
correct answer: At nine, she was reading in bed.
wrong options / checks: At nine, she reads in bed. | At nine, she read the book. | At nine, she has read in bed.
explanation shown to learner: 'At nine' is a moment in the past. The past continuous shows what was in progress then.

task: They ___ TV when I arrived. (watch)
explanation shown to learner: They = were + verb-ing.

task: ___ you ___ at 6 pm? (work)
explanation shown to learner: Question: Were + you + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: He was sleeping. | They were playing. | We weren't listening.
explanation shown to learner: After was/were we need verb-ing: I was watching TV.

task: A friend asks: 'What were you doing at midnight?' Which answer is best?
wrong options / checks: I sleep. | I am sleeping. | I have slept.
explanation shown to learner: The question uses the past continuous, so the answer also describes what was in progress.

task: Write a sentence about what you were doing at 7 pm yesterday. Use was/were + verb-ing.
correct answer: At 7 pm yesterday, I was cooking dinner.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use was or were + verb-ing, for example: I was cooking dinner.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: I ___ along the street when I saw an old friend.
wrong options / checks: walked | am walking | were walking
explanation shown to learner: A longer action in progress (was walking) is interrupted by a short action (saw).

task: In 'When Mia called, I was cooking', which action started first?
correct answer: Cooking. It was already in progress.
wrong options / checks: Calling. | Both at the same moment. | We cannot know.
explanation shown to learner: The past continuous action was already happening when the short action (called) happened.

task: While she ___, her phone ___. (drive / ring)
explanation shown to learner: Long action: was driving. Short action that interrupts: rang.

task: It ___ when we left the house, so we took umbrellas. (rain)
explanation shown to learner: The background situation is in progress: was raining.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: When I was a child, I was playing in the park every day.
wrong options / checks: When I arrived, they were having lunch. | While I was reading, he was watching TV. | She was cooking when the lights went out.
explanation shown to learner: Repeated actions in the past use the past simple (or used to), not the past continuous: I played in the park every day.

task: You tell a story: 'I was walking home. Suddenly a dog ___ out of the garden.' Which form is best?
wrong options / checks: was running | runs | has run
explanation shown to learner: A sudden, short action that interrupts uses the past simple.

task: Write one sentence with 'when' about something that interrupted you. Use the past continuous and the past simple.
correct answer: I was cooking dinner when my friend called.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use was/were + verb-ing for the longer action. ; Use the word when. ; Use the past simple for the short action (rang, arrived, called ...).
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Choose the correct form: I ___ to call you, but my phone died.
wrong options / checks: went | am going | have gone
explanation shown to learner: Was/were going to + base verb = a plan in the past that did not happen.

task: What does 'I was going to call you' mean?
correct answer: I planned to call you, but I didn't.
wrong options / checks: I called you. | I am going to call you now. | I never wanted to call you.
explanation shown to learner: Was going to shows an intention in the past that was not completed.

task: Sorry, I ___ to answer your email, but I was very busy. (go)
explanation shown to learner: Plan in the past: was going to + base verb.

task: While the guests ___, the band ___ quiet music. (arrive / play)
explanation shown to learner: Two actions in progress at the same time: while + past continuous, past continuous.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: They was going to meet us, but they were late.
wrong options / checks: I was going to call you, but I lost your number. | She was going to leave when he arrived. | We were going to stay longer.
explanation shown to learner: They needs were: They were going to meet us.

task: Which sentence best describes a plan that did not happen?
correct answer: We were going to travel to Italy, but we cancelled.
wrong options / checks: We are going to travel to Italy, but we cancelled. | We travel to Italy, but we cancelled. | We have travelled to Italy, but we cancelled.
explanation shown to learner: Past tense + but shows the plan changed: were going to.

task: Write a sentence about a plan you had but did not do. Use was/were going to and but.
correct answer: I was going to go to the gym, but I was too tired.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use was/were going to + base verb. ; Use the word but to say what happened instead.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: I have never ___ sushi.
wrong options / checks: ate | eat | eating
explanation shown to learner: Present perfect = have/has + past participle. The past participle of eat is eaten.

task: Which sentence is about life experience (no exact time)?
wrong options / checks: I went to Spain in 2019. | I'm going to Spain. | I go to Spain every year.
explanation shown to learner: We use the present perfect for experiences up to now when the time is not important.

task: She ___ her homework. (just / finish)
explanation shown to learner: Just goes between has/have and the past participle: has just finished.

task: I haven't ___ her yet. (call)
explanation shown to learner: Negative: haven't + past participle. 'Yet' goes with the present perfect.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I have went to London twice.
wrong options / checks: She has lived here for years. | Have you ever tried Thai food? | We haven't seen that film yet.
explanation shown to learner: The past participle of go is gone (or been for visits): I have been to London twice.

task: Which is the best short answer to: 'Have you ever been to Rome?'
wrong options / checks: Yes, I did. | Yes, I do. | Yes, I am.
explanation shown to learner: Short answers repeat the helper verb of the question: Have you ...? Yes, I have.

task: Write one sentence about something you have never done but would like to do. Use I have never.
correct answer: I have never been to Japan.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use I have never + past participle, for example: I have never been to Japan.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: I've worked here ___ five years.
wrong options / checks: since | from | ago
explanation shown to learner: Use for + a period of time (five years). Use since + a starting point (2020).

task: Which sentence means: it started in the past and is still true now?
correct answer: I have known Tom for ten years.
wrong options / checks: I knew Tom ten years ago. | I know Tom ten years. | I did know Tom for ten years.
explanation shown to learner: The present perfect with for/since connects the past with now.

task: They ___ married for 20 years. (be)
explanation shown to learner: Unfinished period: have been + for 20 years.

task: Make a question with How long: She has worked here since June.
correct answer: How long has she worked here?
explanation shown to learner: How long + has + subject + past participle.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: She has lived here since 2015. | We have known each other for years. | Have you finished yet?
explanation shown to learner: 'Yesterday' is a finished time. Use the past simple: I saw him yesterday.

task: Compare 'I lost my keys' and 'I've lost my keys'. Which one tells us the problem is still there now?
wrong options / checks: I lost my keys. | Both tell us the same. | Neither tells us this.
explanation shown to learner: The present perfect connects the past action with the result now.

task: Write two sentences about how long you have lived in your city or worked in your job. Use for in one and since in the other.
correct answer: I have lived in Riga for ten years. I have worked here since 2020.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use have/has + past participle. ; Use for + a period of time. ; Use since + a start time.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: It's the first time I ___ this dish.
wrong options / checks: tried | try | am trying
explanation shown to learner: After 'It's the first time' we use the present perfect.

task: Which sentence has a finished time word, so we must use the past simple?
correct answer: I saw the film last night.
wrong options / checks: I've seen the film already. | I've seen the film this week. | I've seen the film twice.
explanation shown to learner: 'Last night' is finished, so past simple. Without a finished time we can use the present perfect.

task: How long ___ you ___ English? (study)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: been studying
explanation shown to learner: How long + have + you + past participle (or been + verb-ing).

task: I ___ in three countries, so I speak a little of each language. (live)
explanation shown to learner: Life experience up to now: have + past participle.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: She has just left. | I've known him since 2015. | Have you ever been to Italy?
explanation shown to learner: 'In 2018' is a finished time. Use the past simple: I visited Paris in 2018.

task: A colleague writes: 'I have sent the email yesterday.' Which comment is best?
correct answer: Use the past simple because 'yesterday' is finished: I sent the email yesterday.
wrong options / checks: It is correct. Do not change it. | Use the future: I will send the email yesterday. | Use the past continuous: I was sending the email yesterday.
explanation shown to learner: Finished time words (yesterday, last week, in 2018) need the past simple.

task: Write two sentences: one present perfect about a place you have visited, and one past simple with the time you went.
correct answer: I have been to Lisbon. I went there in 2022.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use the present perfect in the first sentence (have been ...). ; Give a finished time in the second sentence (in 2022, last year, two years ago).
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: I'm tired. I ___ all day.
wrong options / checks: worked | am working | was working
explanation shown to learner: Present perfect continuous = have/has been + verb-ing. It shows an activity over a period up to now.

task: What does 'I've been waiting for an hour' tell us?
correct answer: I started waiting an hour ago. I am still waiting (or I have just stopped).
wrong options / checks: I waited for one hour last week. | I will wait for an hour. | I never wait.
explanation shown to learner: The present perfect continuous shows how long an activity has been happening up to now.

task: She ___ Spanish for six months. (learn)
explanation shown to learner: She + has been + verb-ing.

task: Make a question with How long: They have been waiting.
correct answer: How long have they been waiting?
explanation shown to learner: How long + have + subject + been + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I have been knowing him for years.
wrong options / checks: She has been working here since March. | It has been raining all day. | How long have you been learning English?
explanation shown to learner: 'Know' is a state verb. We say: I have known him for years.

task: Your friend is out of breath because she was running until a minute ago. Which sentence explains why?
wrong options / checks: I run. | I will run. | I ran yesterday.
explanation shown to learner: We use the present perfect continuous to explain a present situation by a recent activity.

task: Write one sentence about something you have been doing a lot lately.
correct answer: I have been studying a lot lately.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use have/has been + verb-ing, for example: I have been studying a lot.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: I ___ this book for two weeks, and I'm still reading it.
wrong options / checks: read | have read | am reading
explanation shown to learner: An activity that started in the past and is still in progress: have been + verb-ing.

task: Which sentence focuses on the result or number (not the activity)?
wrong options / checks: I've been writing emails. | I've been writing for an hour. | I've been writing all morning.
explanation shown to learner: Present perfect simple = result or number. Present perfect continuous = the activity and its duration.

task: Look at the floor! The children ___ with paint. (play)
explanation shown to learner: A recent activity with a visible result: have been playing.

task: I ___ this book all week. I ___ three chapters. (read / finish)
explanation shown to learner: Activity over time: have been reading. Completed result: have finished.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I've been writing five emails today.
wrong options / checks: She has been working here since March. | How long have you been living here? | They have been talking for hours.
explanation shown to learner: With an exact number we use the present perfect simple: I've written five emails today.

task: Your boss asks why you look tired. You were in traffic for an hour until now. Which answer is best?
correct answer: I've been sitting in traffic for an hour.
wrong options / checks: I sit in traffic for an hour. | I will sit in traffic for an hour. | I sat in traffic tomorrow.
explanation shown to learner: A recent, continuing activity that explains the present: present perfect continuous.

task: Write two sentences: one present perfect continuous about an activity, one present perfect simple about a result.
correct answer: I've been studying all week. I've finished two units.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use have/has been + verb-ing in one sentence. ; Use have/has + past participle in the other sentence.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: When we arrived, the film ___ already ___.
wrong options / checks: has ... started | was ... starting | did ... start
explanation shown to learner: Past perfect = had + past participle. It shows an earlier past action.

task: In 'When I got to the station, the train had left', which happened first?
wrong options / checks: I got to the station. | They happened at the same time. | We cannot know.
explanation shown to learner: The past perfect (had left) is the earlier action.

task: She was upset because she ___ her phone. (lose)
explanation shown to learner: The reason came before the feeling: had + past participle.

task: By the time I called, he ___ out. (already / go)
explanation shown to learner: Already goes between had and the past participle: had already gone.

task: Join with After: I finished work. Then I went home.
correct answer: After I had finished work, I went home.
wrong options / checks: also accepted: I went home after I had finished work.
explanation shown to learner: After + past perfect (earlier action), past simple (later action).

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: When I arrived, she already has left.
wrong options / checks: When I arrived, she had already left. | I had never seen snow before that day. | He told me that he had lost his keys.
explanation shown to learner: For an earlier past action use had + past participle: she had already left.

task: Tom arrived at 9. The meeting started at 8.30. Which sentence is correct?
correct answer: When Tom arrived, the meeting had already started.
wrong options / checks: When Tom arrived, the meeting has already started. | When Tom arrived, the meeting would already start. | When Tom arrived, the meeting is already started.
explanation shown to learner: The meeting started before Tom arrived, so we use the past perfect for the meeting.

task: Write one sentence about something that had already happened when you arrived somewhere. Use When I arrived and had already.
correct answer: When I arrived, the film had already started.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use had already + past participle. ; Use When I arrived ... or By the time ...
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: I am ___ to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
wrong options / checks: go | goes | went
explanation shown to learner: Plans: am / is / are + going to + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence is about the future?
correct answer: We are going to eat out tonight.
wrong options / checks: We ate out last night. | We always eat at home. | We are eating now.
explanation shown to learner: Going to + base verb talks about a plan for the future.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Tom ___ a party on Saturday. (have)
explanation shown to learner: A plan: is going to + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: It's cold. I ___ my coat. (take)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: will take
explanation shown to learner: A quick decision now: will + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Make a question: You are going to travel by train.
correct answer: Are you going to travel by train?
explanation shown to learner: Question: Are + you + going to + base verb?

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I going to buy a bike.
wrong options / checks: She is going to cook. | We are going to swim. | They are going to play.
explanation shown to learner: We need am / is / are before going to: I am going to buy a bike.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: A friend asks: 'What are you going to do at the weekend?' Which answer is best?
correct answer: I'm going to visit my parents.
wrong options / checks: I visited my parents. | I visit my parents every day. | I am visit my parents.
explanation shown to learner: The question is about a future plan, so we answer with going to.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Write one sentence about your plan for tomorrow. Use I am going to.
correct answer: I'm going to visit a friend tomorrow.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use I am going to + base verb, for example: I'm going to visit a friend.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.
wrong options / checks: will to | goes to | is going
explanation shown to learner: Going to is used for predictions based on what we can see now: is going to + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence is a plan we made before now?
correct answer: I'm going to start a new course in March.
wrong options / checks: I'll carry your bag. | I think prices will go up. | OK, I'll answer the phone.
explanation shown to learner: Going to shows a plan or intention made before speaking.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: The phone is ringing. - I ___ it. (answer)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: will answer
explanation shown to learner: A decision at the moment of speaking: will + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: We ___ to Rome next month. We've already bought the tickets. (go)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: are going to go
explanation shown to learner: A plan already arranged: are going (to).

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: I'm going to visit my aunt next week. | It will be sunny tomorrow. | She is going to have a baby.
explanation shown to learner: After will we use the base verb without 'to': I will help you.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Black clouds are in the sky. Which sentence is best?
wrong options / checks: It will rain. | It rains. | It rained.
explanation shown to learner: When we see evidence now, going to is the natural choice.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Write a sentence about your plan for next weekend. Use going to.
correct answer: I'm going to visit my parents next weekend.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use am/is/are going to + base verb.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay at home.
wrong options / checks: will rain | is raining | rain
explanation shown to learner: After if, when and as soon as we use the present simple for the future.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence is an arrangement (fixed time and place in your diary)?
correct answer: I'm seeing the dentist at 3 pm on Friday.
wrong options / checks: I'll see the dentist someday. | I will probably see the dentist. | The dentist is nice.
explanation shown to learner: The present continuous with a time shows a fixed arrangement.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: I'll call you when I ___ home. (get)
explanation shown to learner: After when we use the present simple, not will.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Wait! I ___ you with that bag. (help)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: will help
explanation shown to learner: An offer at the moment of speaking: will + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Rewrite with going to: I plan to buy a car.
correct answer: I'm going to buy a car.
wrong options / checks: also accepted: I am going to buy a car.
explanation shown to learner: Going to shows a plan: am going to + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I'll call you when I will arrive.
wrong options / checks: We're flying to Rome on Monday. | I think it'll be a great trip. | As soon as he arrives, we will start.
explanation shown to learner: In time clauses (when, as soon as, before) use the present simple: when I arrive.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Your friend says: 'I will meet Anna at 6, we agreed yesterday.' Which form sounds more natural for an arrangement?
wrong options / checks: I meet Anna at 6 yesterday. | I met Anna at 6 tomorrow. | I'm going to be met Anna at 6.
explanation shown to learner: For arrangements with a time we often use the present continuous.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Write a sentence with when or as soon as about what you will do after class or work.
correct answer: As soon as I finish work, I'll go to the gym.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use when, as soon as, after or before. ; Use will or going to for the later action.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Hurry up! The film ___ to start.
wrong options / checks: is for | goes | will
explanation shown to learner: Be about to + base verb = very soon.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence means something will happen very soon?
correct answer: The plane is about to take off.
wrong options / checks: The plane takes off every day. | The plane took off. | The plane has been taking off.
explanation shown to learner: Be about to is used for the very near future.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Don't worry. I ___ anyone your secret. (not / tell)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: will not tell
explanation shown to learner: A promise: will / won't + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Be careful! You ___ off that chair! (fall)
explanation shown to learner: We can see it is about to happen: are going to + base verb.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: He is going to be arrive soon.
wrong options / checks: She is about to leave. | Will you help me? | It's going to rain; look at the sky.
explanation shown to learner: After going to we use the base verb: He is going to arrive soon.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: You see a colleague with heavy boxes. What is the best offer?
correct answer: I'll carry one of those for you.
wrong options / checks: I carry one of those for you. | I'm carrying one of those for you. | I carried one of those for you.
explanation shown to learner: Will is the natural choice for a spontaneous offer.

tense: Future: will, going to, present continuous
task: Write two sentences: one prediction with going to (with a reason) and one spontaneous offer with will.
correct answer: It's going to rain; look at the clouds. I'll bring an umbrella for you.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use going to + base verb in the prediction. ; Use I'll or I will for the offer.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: English ___ in many countries.
wrong options / checks: speaks | is speak | are spoken
explanation shown to learner: Passive = be + past participle. English is singular, so is spoken.

task: Which sentence is passive?
wrong options / checks: Farmers grow rice in Asia. | People eat rice. | Rice grows in Asia.
explanation shown to learner: In a passive sentence the thing that receives the action is the subject: Rice is grown.

task: Bread ___ from flour. (make)
explanation shown to learner: Passive present simple: is/are + past participle. Bread = it.

task: These cars ___ in Germany. (build)
explanation shown to learner: These cars = they, so are built.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: Cheese is made from milk. | The shops are closed on Sunday. | Letters are delivered every day.
explanation shown to learner: The passive needs the past participle: Coffee is grown in Brazil.

task: Why do we say 'Tickets are sold here'?
correct answer: The action is important. We don't need to say who sells them.
wrong options / checks: Because the tickets are very old. | Because we want to say who sells them. | Because the sentence is in the past.
explanation shown to learner: We use the passive when the action or the object is more important than the person who does it.

task: Write one sentence about a product in your country. Use is made, is grown or are produced.
correct answer: Cheese is made in many parts of Latvia.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use is/are + past participle (is made, are grown ...).
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Where ___ these phones made?
wrong options / checks: do | is | did
explanation shown to learner: Question: be + subject + past participle. These phones = plural, so are.

task: In 'The report is checked by the manager', what is the focus?
correct answer: The report and what happens to it.
wrong options / checks: The manager only. | A future plan. | A past event.
explanation shown to learner: In the passive the subject (the report) is the focus.

task: The office ___ every evening. (clean)
explanation shown to learner: Passive present simple: is + past participle.

task: Change to the passive: They sell fresh bread here.
explanation shown to learner: Object becomes the subject. Verb: is/are + past participle. Fresh bread is sold here.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: Are the tickets checking at the door?
wrong options / checks: Is English taught in your school? | Cars are washed here. | The rooms are cleaned every day.
explanation shown to learner: Passive questions need the past participle: Are the tickets checked at the door?

task: You want to write a neutral email and not blame anyone. Which sentence is best?
correct answer: The invoices are sent on Fridays.
wrong options / checks: You send the invoices on Fridays. | Someone sends the invoices on Fridays. | I think you send the invoices on Fridays.
explanation shown to learner: The passive keeps the focus on the action and does not name a person.

task: Write one sentence about how something is made or done at your workplace. Use the passive.
correct answer: All orders are checked twice before they are sent.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use is/are + past participle.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: ___ English spoken in your office?
wrong options / checks: Does | Do | Are
explanation shown to learner: Passive question: Is + subject + past participle.

task: Which sentence is the passive of 'People often call him Mo'?
wrong options / checks: He often calls Mo. | He is often calling Mo. | Mo is often called him.
explanation shown to learner: The object (him) becomes the subject (He): He is often called Mo.

task: How often ___ the website ___? (update)
explanation shown to learner: Passive question: How often + is + subject + past participle.

task: Change to the passive without 'by': Someone cleans the rooms daily.
wrong options / checks: also accepted: The rooms are cleaned every day.
explanation shown to learner: We leave out the agent (someone) because it is not important.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: The email is send every week.
wrong options / checks: Is this product made in Latvia? | The meetings are held on Mondays. | Many languages are spoken here.
explanation shown to learner: The passive needs the past participle: is sent.

task: Which sentence puts the focus on the data, not on the person?
wrong options / checks: Someone collects the data online. | We collect the data online. | They collect the data online.
explanation shown to learner: The passive moves the focus to the data.

task: Write two sentences about how a product or service in your company is made or delivered. Use the passive and use by in one sentence.
correct answer: The orders are packed in our warehouse. They are delivered by a courier company.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use is/are + past participle. ; Use by + the person or company who does it.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: The Eiffel Tower ___ in 1889.
wrong options / checks: built | is built | were built
explanation shown to learner: Past passive: was/were + past participle. Tower = it, so was built.

task: Which sentence is passive?
wrong options / checks: Someone broke the window. | The window broke. | He is breaking the window.
explanation shown to learner: The window receives the action. Passive: was + broken.

task: The letters ___ yesterday. (send)
explanation shown to learner: Letters = plural, so were + past participle (sent).

task: This picture ___ by Picasso. (paint)
explanation shown to learner: Picture = it, so was painted.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: The book was wrote by Tom.
wrong options / checks: The cake was eaten. | We were invited to the party. | The door was closed.
explanation shown to learner: The past participle of write is written: The book was written by Tom.

task: Which sentence is correct for a past event when we don't know who did it?
wrong options / checks: My bike stole. | My bike was stealing. | My bike were stolen.
explanation shown to learner: Passive past: was/were + past participle. Bike = singular, so was stolen.

task: Write one sentence about a famous building or invention. Use was/were built, invented or discovered.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use was/were + past participle.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: When ___ this museum opened?
wrong options / checks: did | is | has
explanation shown to learner: Passive question in the past: When + was + subject + past participle.

task: Which sentence tells us who did the action?
correct answer: The song was written by Adele.
wrong options / checks: The song was written. | The song is written. | The song writes.
explanation shown to learner: Use by + agent when we want to say who did the action.

task: Where ___ the film ___? (film)
explanation shown to learner: Question: Where + was + subject + past participle.

task: Change to the passive: Someone stole my wallet.
explanation shown to learner: Passive: was + past participle. We leave out 'someone'.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: The thieves were arrested by the police. | The bridge was built in 1998. | I was told the news by Tom.
explanation shown to learner: The past participle of give is given: She was given a prize.

task: A news report says what happened but the person who did it is unknown. Which sentence is best?
correct answer: A car was stolen last night.
wrong options / checks: Someone stealing a car last night. | A car steals last night. | A car were stolen last night.
explanation shown to learner: The passive is common in news reports when the doer is unknown.

task: Write two sentences about something that was done at your workplace last week. Use the passive.
correct answer: A new printer was installed. The old one was thrown away.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use was/were + past participle. ; Write two sentences.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: The documents ___ by the manager yesterday.
wrong options / checks: was signed | signed | are signed
explanation shown to learner: Documents = plural, so were + past participle.

task: Which sentence has the same meaning as 'The police arrested two men'?
correct answer: Two men were arrested (by the police).
wrong options / checks: Two men arrested the police. | Two men are arresting. | Two men were arresting.
explanation shown to learner: Active object (two men) becomes passive subject: Two men were arrested.

task: Our flight ___ because of the storm, so we ___ a hotel room. (cancel / give)
wrong options / checks: also accepted: was canceled
explanation shown to learner: Two passives: was cancelled, were given.

task: Change to the passive: The company hired 20 new workers last year.
correct answer: Twenty new workers were hired last year.
wrong options / checks: also accepted: 20 new workers were hired last year. | Twenty new workers were hired by the company last year. | 20 new workers were hired by the company last year.
explanation shown to learner: New workers is the subject. Was/were + past participle.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: The invoice was send on Monday.
wrong options / checks: The package was delivered yesterday. | The decision was made last week. | We were told to wait.
explanation shown to learner: Use the past participle: The invoice was sent on Monday.

task: You want to mention a mistake politely, without blaming anyone. Which sentence is best?
correct answer: A mistake was made in the report.
wrong options / checks: You made a mistake in the report. | Someone is making a mistake. | I think you make mistakes.
explanation shown to learner: The passive hides the doer and sounds more neutral.

task: Write two sentences to a customer: say what was done to fix a problem. Use the passive.
correct answer: Your order was checked again. A new part was sent to you today.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use was/were + past participle. ; Write two sentences.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: The new bridge ___ at the moment.
wrong options / checks: is building | is built | was being built
explanation shown to learner: Present continuous passive: am/is/are being + past participle.

task: Which sentence means: the work is in progress now?
wrong options / checks: The road was repaired. | The road is repaired every year. | The road will be repaired.
explanation shown to learner: Is being + past participle shows the action is happening now.

task: Please wait. Your order ___. (prepare)
explanation shown to learner: Order = it. In progress now: is being prepared.

task: The rooms ___ right now. (clean)
explanation shown to learner: Rooms = plural: are being cleaned.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: The hotel is being renovated. | The cars are being washed now. | My email is being checked.
explanation shown to learner: Use the past participle: The report is being written.

task: A technician is still working on your computer. What is the best sentence?
wrong options / checks: Your computer is fixed. | Your computer was fixed. | Your computer fixes.
explanation shown to learner: 'Is fixed' means the job is finished. 'Is being fixed' means it is in progress.

task: Write one sentence about something that is being built, repaired or changed in your area now. Use is/are being.
correct answer: A new shopping centre is being built near my house.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use is/are being + past participle.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: My car ___ repaired, so I can drive again.
wrong options / checks: have been | is been | has being
explanation shown to learner: Present perfect passive: has/have been + past participle.

task: Which sentence is the passive of 'They have finished the project'?
wrong options / checks: The project have been finished. | The project has finished. | The project is being finished.
explanation shown to learner: has been + finished. Project is singular, so has.

task: All the tickets ___. (sell)
explanation shown to learner: Tickets = plural, so have been sold.

task: Change to the passive: Someone has stolen my bag.
explanation shown to learner: has been + past participle.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: The windows have been cleaned. | The room has been booked. | Has the letter been sent?
explanation shown to learner: Rooms is plural, so have been prepared.

task: Which sentence tells us the email is now available to check?
wrong options / checks: The email was sent. | The email will be sent. | The email is sending.
explanation shown to learner: The present perfect passive links the past action with now.

task: Write a sentence about something that has been done at your home or office this week. Use has/have been + past participle.
correct answer: The windows have been cleaned this week.
wrong options / checks: must contain: Use has/have been + past participle.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: ___ the problem been solved yet?
wrong options / checks: Is | Have | Did
explanation shown to learner: Question: Has + subject + been + past participle.

task: Which sentence sounds like news that is important right now?
correct answer: The road has been closed because of the accident.
wrong options / checks: The road was closed in 1999. | The road closes every night. | The road is closing.
explanation shown to learner: The present perfect passive is used for recent news with a result now.

task: Several mistakes ___ in the report so far. (find)
explanation shown to learner: So far = up to now: have been found.

task: Change to the passive: They have already sent the invoice.
correct answer: The invoice has already been sent.
explanation shown to learner: Already goes between has and been.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
wrong options / checks: The decision has been made. | Has the form been signed? | The package has been delivered.
explanation shown to learner: We need been: The room has been cleaned.

task: Compare 'The bridge was closed' and 'The bridge has been closed'. Which one tells us the bridge is probably still closed now?
wrong options / checks: The bridge was closed. | Both tell us the same. | Neither tells us this.
explanation shown to learner: Present perfect = connection with now.

task: Write two sentences about changes that have been made in your company, school or city. Use has/have been + past participle at least once.

wrong options / checks: must contain: Use has/have been + past participle. ; Write two sentences.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: Your parcel ___ tomorrow.
wrong options / checks: will deliver | is deliver | will be deliver
explanation shown to learner: Future passive: will be + past participle.

task: Which sentence is a prediction about what will happen to the road?

wrong options / checks: The new road was opened last year. | The new road opens every day. | The new road is opening.
explanation shown to learner: Will be + past participle looks forward and focuses on the road.

task: The results ___ on Friday. (announce)
explanation shown to learner: will be + past participle.

task: Change to the passive: They will open the shop at 9.

explanation shown to learner: will be + past participle.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?

explanation shown to learner: Use the past participle: The prize will be given to the winner.

task: You do not want to say who will do the action. Which sentence is best?

wrong options / checks: Someone checks the files on Monday. | The files check on Monday. | The files will checking on Monday.
explanation shown to learner: The passive keeps the focus on the files.

task: Write one sentence about something that will be done in your city or company next year. Use will be + past participle.

wrong options / checks: must contain: Use will be + past participle.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

task: ___ the new rules be explained to us?
wrong options / checks: Do | Are | Have
explanation shown to learner: Passive question: Will + subject + be + past participle.

task: Which sentence is the passive of 'They will announce the winner tomorrow'?
correct answer: The winner will be announced tomorrow.
wrong options / checks: The winner will announce tomorrow. | The winner is announcing tomorrow. | The winner was announced tomorrow.
explanation shown to learner: will + be + past participle.

task: Don't worry. Everything ___ before the guests arrive. (prepare)
explanation shown to learner: will be + past participle.

task: Change to the passive: We will send the tickets by email.
correct answer: The tickets will be sent by email.
explanation shown to learner: will be + past participle.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?

explanation shown to learner: Use the past participle: The class will be cancelled.

explanation shown to learner: Announcements often use the passive: will be informed.

wrong options / checks: must contain: Use will be + past participle. ; Write two sentences.
explanation shown to learner: Compare your sentence with the model answer.
